_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season10-bible-v1.0.1.md row a10e10, writer brief a10e10-v1.0.0.md, LATENT catalog v1.0.80 and latent-syllabus-v1.0.3.md. a10e09's file appeared while this case was written; only its next field was read and it is honoured (The Cost of a Token, a tyre factory's night shift: the cost of a million tokens, how busy the cards really are, adding and removing cards with the load, renting a model by the token against running your own). The last LATENT case: its next field points to Season 10's 3 AM Interview, and the course ends there. No conveyor, bottles, ledger, accountant, per-request cloud function or counting house; curing presses are never called ovens; the furnace appears only as the season's comparison. Shared given data: Llama 3.1 8B, 16.06 billion bytes, about 15 GB on the card's meter; the writing curve on one A100 80GB (10 ms a step plus 0.25 ms an answer), Velsham's own measurement; two A100 80GB cards at $2.79 a card hour, $5.58 an hour, $4,073 a month of 730 hours. Story arithmetic (all in sims/a10e10-v1.0.0.js): day 32 a card, 18 ms, 1,778 a second a card, 12.8 million an hour, $0.44 per million; night 12 a card, 13 ms, 923, 6.65 million an hour, $0.84; the meter 100% on both; one card for 24, 16 ms, 62.5 each, 1,500 in all, 5.4 million an hour, $0.52; a night at the report's pace 53.17 million tokens x $0.14 = $7.44 (answers only) against $22.32 for one card's night; a third card 12 ms, 667 a card, $1.16, $6,110 a month; about 10% off ($2.51) $0.76 at night, $409 a month saved. Two deliberate changes from the brief: (1) the saving. The brief's 8 x $2.79 x 30 = $670 assumes the second card off for all 8 hours and a 30-night month; the case starts it at 05:50 (ready 05:53) and the rental bills by the minute, so it is off 7 h 50 min: $21.86 a night, and with the case's 730-hour month (30.4 nights) $665 a month. (2) The option texts: option 0 says off at 22:00, on at 05:50, and options 2 and 3 name two companies apart (a provider that charges per token; the rental company and its hourly price), as a8e07 did. Answers at once are a closed count: a running note is rewritten as soon as it is done, so the number written at once follows the presses and crews on shift, and tokens an hour follow the speed. Timeline: three night lines to 00:00 Monday 5 October 2026 (the report for Monday 28 September to Sunday 4 October); one since; the weekly cost report, emailed by Mstislav's script, for Monday 5 to Sunday 11 October at 00:00 Monday 12 October; the post at about 03:00; the change live at 22:00 Monday 12 October; card 2 on at 05:50 Tuesday 13 October, taking answers at 05:53. Cold case: 2 months later, 12 October to 12 December 2026: two night lines back at 22:00 Monday 7 December, 64 at once on one card, 26 ms, 38.5 tokens a second each, 2,462 a card, $0.31 per million. Standards note conditional, not legal advice. Sources read 16 October 2026; the PDPC page's text did not come through the fetcher, so it is cited by name only.
title: The Cost of a Token

post.author: u/night_office_ferdous
post.title: I run a tyre factory's night shift and the assistant's budget. Tonight's report says both our cards were 100% busy all night, and each token cost nearly twice as much.

blocks.text: I'm Ferdous, night shift manager at Velsham Tyres, and I own the budget line for our assistant. It keeps a running note for each curing press, the heated mould that sets a tyre, and answers the crews' questions.

The assistant is a language model, a program that writes text one token at a time. A token is a small piece of a word. Ours is Llama 3.1 8B: 16.06 billion bytes of learned numbers, about 15 GB, billions of bytes.

It runs on two rented NVIDIA A100 80GB graphics cards, cards for short: chips of tiny adders fed by one fast memory road. Our rental company bills $2.79 a card hour, by the minute, while a card is on. Ours never switch off: $5.58 an hour, $4,073 a month of 730 hours.

The model writes in steps. In each step a card reads all 16.06 billion bytes once, and every answer in the step gets one more token. Mstislav, our IT contractor, timed it: 10 ms, thousandths of a second, plus 0.25 ms for each answer in the step.

A note is rewritten as soon as it's done, so how many are written at once follows the presses and crews on shift. By day three press lines run: 64 answers at once, 32 per card. A step takes 10 ms + 32 × 0.25 ms = 18 ms for 32 tokens: 1,778 tokens a second per card, 12.8 million tokens an hour from both.

A rented card costs the same every hour, like a furnace that burns the same fuel whether the ladle is full or half empty. So I divide the hour's price by the millions of tokens written in it: the cost per million tokens. By day, $5.58 ÷ 12.8 million = $0.44 per million.

Each card also has a meter, its utilisation. Many times a minute it takes a sample, a look lasting between a sixth of a second and a second, and asks one question: did any work run on the card, yes or no? It reports the share of yes.

Mstislav's script emails me a weekly cost report every Monday at 00:00. Tonight's, for Monday 5 to Sunday 11 October, reached me in the night office. Each line gives a figure and, where it changed, the week before's. GPU, short for graphics processing unit, means the card's chip.

GPU utilisation                  100% on both cards, day and night
night tokens a second per card   923, down from 1,778
night cost per million tokens    $0.84, up from $0.44

Nights used to be as busy as days. Then our biggest customer cut its winter order, and at 00:00 on Monday 5 October two of three night lines stopped. The report for 28 September to 4 October still had three; this is the first with one.

One line means 24 answers at once, 12 per card. By hand: 10 ms + 12 × 0.25 ms = 13 ms a step for 12 tokens, 923 tokens a second per card, about 6.65 million tokens an hour from both: $5.58 ÷ 6.65 million = $0.84 per million.
About half the tokens, the same full meter, the same $5.58 an hour.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in your night office is haunted, though a meter stuck at 100% is a grim thing to read at midnight. Your step time is also the gap each crew waits between one token and the next (a10e02): 18 ms by day, 13 ms tonight. Two questions. Of tonight's 13 ms step, how much is the card reading the model, and how much is the 12 answers? And in one of the meter's samples, what does it say during a step with 12 answers, and during one with 32?

replies.author: u/night_office_ferdous
replies.text: Reading is 10 ms either way. The answers take 3 ms tonight and 8 ms by day. The meter says yes to both: some work was running. A step with 12 answers and a step with 32 look the same to it.

comments.author: u/more_capacity_tarquin
comments.text: Production manager. 100% on both cards is the definition of needing more capacity. A machine that runs flat out all night has no headroom, and the winter order will come back. Rent a third card now, while the rental company has them. And if each step is the problem, find a card with more TFLOPS, trillions of sums a second, so it finishes sooner.

replies.author: u/night_office_ferdous
replies.text: The meter read 100% last week too, when the cards wrote nearly twice the tokens.

replies.author: u/more_capacity_tarquin
replies.text: Then they were full last week as well. Either way, there's no headroom.

comments.author: u/hourly_rate_kofoworola
comments.text: Finance. Those cards run all 730 hours of every month, and a steady customer gets a better hourly price. Before anyone touches the set-up, I'll ask the rental company for about 10% off: $2.51 instead of $2.79 a card hour, on every hour, day and night.

replies.author: u/hourly_rate_kofoworola
replies.text: It brings it down. Every cent off the hour comes off every token.

comments.author: u/per_token_bheki
comments.text: Process engineer. Why rent cards for the night at all? A provider, a company that runs models and sells their use, offers an 8B Llama as a per-token service: we'd pay for each token sent in and written out, and nothing for quiet hours. One lists $0.14 per million tokens, in and out. At the report's night pace we write about 53 million tokens a night: about $7.44 for the answers, against $44.64 for our two cards' night.

replies.author: u/night_office_ferdous
replies.text: The press notes carry our cure recipes and the crews' names. They would leave the factory under the provider's terms, and if any of it is personal data, facts about a person who can be named, a transfer rule may apply, such as the transfer limitation obligation in Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA). That's for someone who knows the law; this isn't legal advice.

comments.author: u/start_up_mstislav
comments.text: IT contractor. For the record: the cards are rented by the minute, and either one can be switched off from the rental company's page. Switching one back on takes about 3 minutes: the card starts, the model's 15 GB is copied onto it, then it takes answers. We've never done it, because nights were always busy.

reply.prompt: It's 03:00 on Monday 12 October. The next night shift starts at 22:00 tonight, and the day lines at 06:00 on Tuesday. What should Velsham change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Count tokens per card; turn the second card off at 22:00, on at 05:50.
options.part2: On Monday Mstislav changed the weekly report to lead with tokens a second per card and cost per million, with the meter last, and set card 2 on the rental company's page to switch off at 22:00 and on at 05:50. The script now also phones me if card 2 isn't taking answers by 05:56. At 22:00 on Monday 12 October card 2 switched off and its bill stopped; card 1 took every note and answer. In the sim: 10 ms + 24 × 0.25 ms = 16 ms a step, 1,500 tokens a second, 5.4 million an hour, $2.79 ÷ 5.4 million = $0.52 per million. Each note and answer came at 62.5 tokens a second, down from 76.9 on two cards since 5 October and still faster than the day's 55.6; no crew noticed. For eight hours there was no spare card: had card 1 failed, the night would have waited at least 3 minutes for card 2. It didn't. At 05:50 on Tuesday card 2 switched on, and at 05:53 it was taking answers, seven minutes before the day lines. Card 2's night cost $0.47 instead of $22.32: $21.86 a night saved, $665 a month of 730 hours. The meter on card 1 read 100% all night.
options.senior: Measure capacity in work done: tokens a second per card and cost per million at the fill you really get. The meter only asks whether any work ran in each sample, so a step with 12 answers reads as busy as a step with 32, and it can never tell you a card is half empty. At night one card holds all 24 answers in fuller steps: each step a little longer, 16 ms against 13, each answer a little slower, and each token cheaper, $0.52 per million against $0.84. That is autoscaling in its simplest form: the number of cards follows the load, with a floor of one card and a start time early enough to cover the 3-minute start-up. A clock is the simplest trigger; a load trigger, answers at once per card, is safer when the night changes. It will not reach the day's $0.44, because 24 answers on one card fill a step less than 32 do.

options.text: Rent a third card, since the meter shows both cards 100% busy all night.
options.part2: Tarquin signed on Monday for a third A100 at $2.79 a card hour, always on like the others. From 22:00 the night's 24 answers were spread over three cards, 8 a card. In the sim: 10 ms + 8 × 0.25 ms = 12 ms a step, 667 tokens a second a card, 7.2 million tokens an hour, $8.37 ÷ 7.2 million = $1.16 per million, up from $0.84. The bill rose to $6,110 a month, $2,037 more. Each answer at night came at 83.3 tokens a second instead of 76.9, a speed no crew had asked for. The next Monday's report said 100% on all three cards, day and night.
options.senior: A busy meter is not a full card. The meter asks only whether any work ran in each sample, so it reads 100% on a step with 8 answers just as on one with 32. A third card spreads the same 24 answers thinner: emptier steps, each paying the same 10 ms to read the model, so each token costs more. Size by tokens a second per card against what a full step can do, and keep headroom as a plan to start a card when the load comes, not as a card that idles in steps a quarter full.

options.text: Send the night's work to a provider that charges per token, not by hour.
options.verdict: Trade-off: cheaper nights, the data leaves
options.part2: Bheki set it up on Monday: from 22:00 the night's notes and questions went to the provider, both cards switched off, and both switched back on at 05:50, taking answers at 05:53. First Mstislav ran a week of press readings through the provider's model, because its list says Llama 3 8B Instruct Lite, not our Llama 3.1 8B, and a different model needs re-testing (a6e09). Its notes were worded differently, so the cure times were checked by hand that night. The provider charged about $7.44 for the night's answers, about 53 million tokens, against $22.32 for one card of our own; the prompts, the press readings sent in, were charged at the same $0.14 per million on top, and nobody had counted them. In the sim, before prompts: $2,970 a month, $1,103 less. And every press note, with its cure recipe and the crew's names, now left the factory under the provider's terms. Kofoworola sent the terms to the company's lawyer to read for any transfer rule; that reading is theirs, and this is not legal advice.
options.senior: An honest sum: per token, a provider charges only for what you send and write, so a quiet night costs little, $7.44 for the answers against $22.32 for one of our own cards. Count the prompts too, which are charged at the same rate, before trusting the gap; a8e07's break-even still holds, and the busier our cards, the more they win. And the price is not the whole decision. The press data leaves the factory under the provider's terms, where a transfer rule such as Singapore's PDPA transfer limitation obligation may apply to any personal data (not legal advice), and the listed model is not ours, so it must be re-tested on our own notes before it writes them.

options.text: Ask the rental company for a lower hourly price; the cards run all night.
options.verdict: Cheaper hours, the same empty steps
options.part2: Kofoworola rang the rental company on Monday morning. It offered about 10% off, $2.51 a card hour, if we kept both cards for a year, and Kofoworola signed. The nights didn't change: 12 answers a card, 13 ms a step, 923 tokens a second a card. In the sim the cost per million fell to $0.76 at night and $0.39 by day, and the bill to $3,665 a month, $409 less. The next Monday's report still said 100% on both cards, day and night, and a night token still cost nearly twice a day one, now for a year: both cards are paid for all night until October 2027.
options.senior: A lower hourly price takes the same share off every token, so it helps, but it leaves the cause alone: at night each card pays its 10 ms of reading for 12 answers instead of 32. Cost per million is price per hour ÷ millions of tokens per hour; the price fell about 10%, but the night's tokens per hour stayed about half the day's. And a year's commitment fixes the number of cards just when the load says it should change. Fix the fill first, then talk about price.

sim.title: Run Velsham's cards through a night
sim.lede: You're Ferdous at 23:59:50 on Sunday 11 October in the night office, ten seconds before the weekly cost report arrives. No real model runs here: every figure is worked out from given numbers. Given: Llama 3.1 8B, 16.06 billion bytes, about 15 GB; two rented NVIDIA A100 80GB cards at $2.79 a card hour, billed by the minute while on; a month is 730 hours, about 30.4 nights. Velsham's own measurements, never a source's: a step takes 10 ms plus 0.25 ms for each answer in it; 64 answers at once by day, 24 at night since 00:00 on Monday 5 October (64 before); a card switched on takes about 3 minutes before it takes answers. Night is 22:00 to 06:00. Prices are close to one provider's list on 16 October 2026: a per-token service at $0.14 per million tokens, priced here on the answers alone, at the report's night pace.
sim.tryThis: Try this: the opening view is tonight: 24 answers at once at night on two cards, 13 ms a step, 923 tokens a second a card, $0.84 per million, the meter at 100%. Play the report. Set the night to 64 answers to see last week: 18 ms and $0.44 with the same meter. Play each reply. Then run one card at night with the second started at 05:50, and again at 06:00. Last, put 64 answers at night on one card and watch each answer slow down while the cost per million falls.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the night office was haunted. The meter only asks whether any work ran in each sample, so a 13 ms step carrying 12 answers reads as busy as an 18 ms step carrying 32. At night each card wrote 923 tokens a second instead of 1,778, for the same $2.79 an hour: $5.58 ÷ 6.65 million = $0.84 per million, against $0.44 by day.

steps.title: One step, many answers.
steps.text: Writing goes in steps. First, the card reads the whole model, 16.06 billion bytes, along its memory road: 10 ms on Velsham's own timing, whatever the step holds. Second, every answer in the step gets one more token, 0.25 ms each. Third, the next step starts. So one reading serves every answer in the step (a10e01, a10e04). By day 32 answers share each step: 10 ms + 32 × 0.25 ms = 18 ms for 32 tokens, 1,778 tokens a second a card. At night 12 share it: 13 ms for 12 tokens, 923 a second. The night's step is 72% as long as the day's and carries three-eighths of its tokens. What can go wrong: a half-empty step still pays the whole 10 ms of reading.

steps.title: Cost per million tokens, at the fill you really get.
steps.text: A rented card costs the same every hour, like a furnace that burns the same fuel whether the ladle is full or half empty. First, take what the cards cost in an hour: $5.58 for two. Second, count the tokens they wrote in that hour, in millions: 12.8 by day, 6.65 at night. Third, divide: $0.44 per million by day, $0.84 at night. Nothing about the cards changed; only how full each step was. One card carrying all 24 night answers writes 1,500 tokens a second, 5.4 million an hour: $2.79 ÷ 5.4 million = $0.52. A third card spreads the 24 thinner: 7.2 million an hour for $8.37, $1.16. This is a6e04's cost per request and Dead Letter s9e04's cost per unit of business, worked from card hours. What can go wrong: quoting a cost per million measured at a full test load when the real steps are half empty.

steps.title: What the meter measures.
steps.text: NVIDIA's nvidia-smi tool defines GPU utilisation as the percent of time over the past sample period during which one or more kernels was executing on the GPU; a kernel is one piece of work the card runs. First, the meter takes a sample, between a sixth of a second and a second long depending on the card. Second, it asks one question: did any kernel run in it, yes or no? Third, it reports the share of yes. Steps run back to back while any answer is being written, so the meter reads 100% at 8 answers, at 12 and at 32. It measures time busy, not work done. What can go wrong: buying cards because a meter that cannot see how full the steps are says 100%.

steps.title: Autoscaling: the number of cards follows the load.
steps.text: Autoscaling changes how many cards run as the load changes, with a floor and a start-up time; Dead Letter's s6e11 scaled workers the same way. First, measure the load in work: answers at once per card, or tokens a second per card. Second, when one card can carry it, here 24 answers in 16 ms steps, one card takes every answer at 22:00 and the other switches off; the floor is one card. Third, before the load rises, start the second card early enough for its start-up: at 05:50 it switches on, the model's 15 GB is copied onto it in about 3 minutes, and it takes answers at 05:53, before the day lines at 06:00. Started at 06:00 it would be 3 minutes late. Saved: 7 h 50 min × $2.79 = $21.86 a night, $665 a month of 730 hours. What can go wrong: a rule set by the clock alone keeps one card when the load comes back at night, and with one card there is no spare for at least 3 minutes if it fails.

steps.title: A per-token service or our own cards: a sum plus the terms.
steps.text: First, price the night on the service: 53.17 million tokens × $0.14 per million = $7.44 for the answers, before the prompts, which are charged too. Second, price it on our own cards at their real fill: one card's night is 8 h × $2.79 = $22.32. Third, compare, remembering a8e07's break-even: the busier our cards, the more they win. Then add the part the sum leaves out. The press data leaves the factory under the provider's terms, where a transfer rule such as Singapore's PDPA transfer limitation obligation may apply to any personal data (not legal advice). And the listed model, Llama 3 8B Instruct Lite, is not our Llama 3.1 8B, so it is re-tested on our own notes first (a6e09). What can go wrong: comparing the answers' price with the cards' and forgetting the prompts and the terms.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for one night. Top row: at 22:00 card 2 switches off and its bill stops; card 1 alone carries 24 answers in 16 ms steps, 1,500 tokens a second; $0.52 per million, was $0.84, each answer 62.5 tokens a second. Bottom row: at 05:50 card 2 switches on and the model is copied in about 3 minutes; at 05:53 it takes answers, 7 minutes to spare; from 06:00 the day runs 32 answers a card in 18 ms steps at $0.44 per million.

notes.text: The fix: one card at night, the second back before 06:00
Count tokens per card; the meter reads 100% either way

explain.caption: Read each row left to right. Top: at 22:00 card 2 switches off and card 1 carries all 24 answers in fuller steps, so each token costs less. Bottom: card 2 switches on at 05:50, takes answers by 05:53, and both cards carry the day from 06:00.

fix.title: The fix: count tokens per card, and run one card at night
fix.text: Lead the weekly report with tokens a second per card and cost per million, and keep the meter only as a sign that a card is on. Set card 2 to switch off at 22:00 and on at 05:50, and have the script check at 05:56 that it is taking answers and phone the night shift manager if not. The floor is one card, card 1, which carries the night's 24 answers in 16 ms steps at $0.52 per million. Before any per-token service, price the prompts as well as the answers, read the provider's terms for the press data, and re-test the provider's model on our own notes.

limits: The writing curve, the 3-minute start-up, the answers at once and the night's tokens are Velsham's own measurements, not a source's, and the per-minute billing is story data. The prices are close to one provider's list on 16 October 2026; they change, and the arithmetic is the lesson.

A clock is the simplest trigger and the bluntest: if the night lines come back, one card carries every answer in longer steps until someone changes the times. And for eight hours there is no spare card; if card 1 fails, answers wait at least 3 minutes for card 2.
The per-token figure counts the answers alone. The prompts are charged too, and the service's own speed was never measured here.

explain.seniorTake: Cost per million tokens is price per hour ÷ millions of tokens per hour, and the tokens per hour depend on how full each step is, because one reading of the model serves every answer in the step. That is why a busy fleet can pay nearly twice as much per token at night: the cards cost the same, and the steps are half empty. The meter cannot show it; it counts time busy, not work done, so a step with 12 answers reads 100% just as one with 32. Size and scale the fleet on work: tokens a second per card, answers at once per card, cost per million at real fill. Then let the number of cards follow the load, with a floor and a start-up time, and treat a per-token service as a sum plus its terms: the prompts, the data leaving, and a model that must be re-tested. The meter runs while the card waits; tonight it ran on half-empty steps, and the sum by hand shows it: $5.58 ÷ 6.65 million = $0.84.

realWorld.title: nvidia-smi: what utilisation counts
realWorld.text: NVIDIA's nvidia-smi documentation defines GPU utilisation as: Percent of time over the past sample period during which one or more kernels was executing on the GPU. The definition counts time with work running, not how much of the card that work used.

realWorld.title: nvidia-smi: the sample
realWorld.text: The same page says: The sample period may be between 1 second and 1/6 second depending on the product. Each sample answers one question, whether any kernel ran in it.

realWorld.title: What the cards cost
realWorld.text: Lambda's pricing page, read on 16 October 2026, lists the NVIDIA A100 SXM with 80 GB at $2.79 per GPU per hour, plus applicable sales tax/VAT/GST. Velsham's $2.79 is given data close to that list, not Lambda's offer to the factory, and the page states no billing increment; the per-minute billing is the story's. Prices change; the arithmetic is the lesson.

realWorld.title: What a per-token service costs
realWorld.text: Together AI's pricing page, read on 16 October 2026, lists Llama 3 8B Instruct Lite at $0.14 input and $0.14 output, price per 1M tokens. That is not Llama 3.1 8B, so a team switching to it re-tests it first. 53.17 million night tokens × $0.14 = $7.44 for the answers alone.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 A1.1: capacity in use
realWorld.text: A third-party page gives SOC 2 criterion A1.1 as: The entity maintains, monitors, and evaluates current processing capacity and use of system components, with Measures Current Usage among its points of focus. A meter that counts time busy measures the time, not the use.

asked: How do you compute cost per million tokens for a self-hosted model?
Why is GPU utilization a misleading metric?
When is an API cheaper than your own GPUs?
interview.answer: Cost per million is the price per GPU hour times the GPUs, divided by the millions of tokens they produce in that hour at your real load, not a benchmark's. Tokens per hour depend on batch fill: a decode step reads the weights once for every request in the batch, so a step with 32 requests costs little more than one with 12 but yields almost three times the tokens. In one example, two A100s at $2.79 an hour gave $0.44 per million with 32 requests per GPU and $0.84 with 12. GPU utilization, as nvidia-smi reports it, is the percent of time any kernel was running in the sample period, so it reads 100% on a half-empty batch; it measures time busy, not work done. Size and autoscale on tokens per second per GPU, requests in flight and cost per million, with a floor and a start-up time: in the example, one GPU at night with the second started ten minutes before the morning load saved $665 a month. An API wins when your GPUs would sit idle or half full: compare its per-token price, input and output, with your cost per million at real fill, then add what the sum leaves out: data leaving under the provider's terms, any transfer rules for personal data, and a different model that must be re-evaluated before switching.

A small piece of text, often part of a word, that a model reads and writes (a1e03).
Meta's language model with 8.03 billion learned numbers, two bytes each: 16.06 billion bytes, about 15 GB on the card's meter. Velsham runs its own copy.
A byte holds 8 bits. A GB is about a billion bytes; the card's meter counts 1 GB as 1,024 MB, while speeds use the maker's 1,000.
Short for graphics card: a board with a GPU and its own memory (a10e01). Velsham rents two.
Graphics processing unit, the chip on a card: thousands of tiny adders fed by one fast memory road. The report says GPU for the card.
The card Velsham rents: 80 GB of memory, at $2.79 a card hour in the story.
This season's word for the link that carries the model's numbers from the card's memory to its adders (a10e01). Every step travels it once.
The company Velsham rents its cards from, billed by the minute while a card is on, at $2.79 a card hour.
One card switched on for one hour: $2.79 here. Two cards always on cost $5.58 an hour, $4,073 a month of 730 hours.
What the rental company charges for a card hour, whatever the card does in it.
One pass of writing: the card reads the model once and every answer in the step gets one more token (a10e04).
A millisecond, a thousandth of a second. A step took 18 ms by day and 13 ms at night.
Velsham's own timing of one A100: a step takes 10 ms plus 0.25 ms for each answer in it. 12 answers: 13 ms; 24: 16 ms; 32: 18 ms.
How many notes and answers a card is writing in the same step. 32 a card by day, 12 at night since 5 October.
How many tokens a card writes each second, across every answer in its steps: answers ÷ step time. 1,778 by day, 923 at night.
Price per hour ÷ millions of tokens written in that hour. $5.58 ÷ 12.8 = $0.44 by day, $0.84 at night: the fuller the step, the cheaper the token.
The card's busy meter. In each sample it asks whether any work ran, yes or no, and reports the share of yes. It reads 100% on full and half-empty steps alike.
One short look by the meter, between a sixth of a second and a second long, depending on the card.
One piece of work the card runs, such as part of a step. The meter counts a sample as busy if any kernel was running.
NVIDIA's command-line tool that reports a card's state, including its utilisation.
The email Mstislav's script sends Ferdous every Monday at 00:00: the meter, tokens a second per card and cost per million for the week before.
Trillions of sums a second, a card's top adding speed (a10e01). Writing a token waits on the memory road, so more TFLOPS barely helps.
A company that runs models on its own computers and sells their use, billed by the token (a6e04).
A provider's model used over the internet and charged for each token sent and written, nothing for quiet hours (a8e07). One lists an 8B Llama at $0.14 per million.
The text sent to the model with each request: the press readings or a crew's question. A per-token service charges for it too.
The 8B Llama on one provider's price list, $0.14 per million tokens in and out. It is not Velsham's Llama 3.1 8B, so it needs re-testing.
Running your own test set on a different model before switching to it (a6e09).
From switching a card on to its first answer: the card starts and the model's 15 GB is copied onto it. About 3 minutes at Velsham.
Changing the number of cards with the load, with a floor and a start-up time: one card at night, two from 05:50. Dead Letter's s6e11 scaled workers the same way.
The fewest cards that stay on whatever the load. Velsham's is one.
A rule that starts or stops a card when the load passes a line, such as answers at once per card, rather than at a set time.
The volume at which two ways of paying cost the same per token (a8e07).
Information about a person who can be identified, such as a crew member's name.
Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act 2012. Its transfer limitation obligation sets conditions for sending personal data out of Singapore.
The PDPA's rule on sending personal data outside Singapore. Whether it applies depends on the data and the place; not legal advice.
A company that rents GPUs by the hour. Its price list shows an A100 80GB at $2.79 per GPU an hour.
A provider whose price list shows Llama 3 8B Instruct Lite at $0.14 per million tokens, in and out.
Singapore's Data Protection Trustmark: a certification that an organisation's handling of personal data meets a set standard.
The international standard for information security management. Its Annex A lists controls such as 8.6 capacity management and 5.23 cloud services.
Annex A 8.6: watching and planning the resources a system needs now and later.
An auditor's report on a company's controls. Criterion A1.1 covers measuring and evaluating processing capacity and its use.
The international standard for quality management. Clause 7.1.5 covers monitoring and measuring resources.
The course's hands-on builds. The Nightwatch copilot's X6 reuses this case: cost per million tokens at real fill.

atWork: Look for a fleet of rented or owned GPUs sized by its utilisation meter: a dashboard that reads 100% day and night, and a request for more cards that cites it. It is a common pattern: the meter counts time busy, so it reads full on half-empty steps, and nobody sees the cost per token rise when the load falls. Ask four things. How many requests share each step on each card, by hour of day? What does each card write in tokens a second, and what is the cost per million at that fill? How many cards would carry the quiet hours, what is the floor, and how long does a card take from switch-on to its first answer? And if a per-token service is cheaper on paper, have you counted the prompts, read its terms for your data, and re-tested its model? The Nightwatch copilot's X6 build reuses this case: cost per million at real fill. Standards-readiness note, stated conditionally and not legal advice: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, an auditor checking Annex A 8.6 (capacity management, as summarised by a third-party guide) would look for capacity measured in work done, not a busy meter, and one checking Annex A 5.23 (cloud services) and the supplier controls 5.19 to 5.22 would look for the per-token provider's terms read before any data went to it. Under SOC 2, criterion A1.1 says the entity maintains, monitors, and evaluates current processing capacity and use of system components, so an auditor would look for use measured, not only time. Under ISO 9001:2015, clause 7.1.5 covers monitoring and measuring resources; a third-party guide says all measurement devices must be verified before they can be used to provide reliable data, and a meter that cannot see how full a step is may not pass that check. For Singapore's DPTM, the PDPA's transfer limitation obligation would apply if personal data, such as crew names, went to a provider outside Singapore. As they apply to you; this is not legal advice.

recall.prompt: Your company serves its own model on eight rented GPUs, always on. The monitoring page shows GPU utilisation at 98% around the clock, and a manager asks for budget for eight more before the holiday rush. Overnight traffic is about a third of the day's. What do you check before agreeing, and what would you propose?

keyIdeas.idea: Utilisation only says some work ran in each sample, so it reads near 100% on half-empty steps: it measures time busy, not work done
Measure tokens a second per GPU and cost per million tokens (price per hour ÷ millions of tokens an hour) at the real fill
Scale the number of GPUs with the load: fewer overnight, down to a floor, started again early enough for their start-up

recall.model: Utilisation only says some work ran in each sample, so it reads near 100% on half-empty steps: it measures time busy, not work done. Before buying, I'd measure tokens a second per GPU and requests per step by hour, and work out cost per million (price per hour ÷ millions of tokens an hour) at that real fill; overnight it will be well above the day's. Then I'd propose autoscaling: switch off GPUs overnight down to a floor that carries the quiet hours, and start them again early enough for their start-up before the morning, and judge the result in tokens, not on the meter.

recall.prompt: Two rented cards at $2.79 an hour each write 6.65 million tokens an hour between them. What is the cost per million tokens?
recall.why: $5.58 an hour ÷ 6.65 million = $0.84. $0.42 is one card's $2.79 ÷ 6.65; $0.44 is the day's $5.58 ÷ 12.8 million; $1.19 divides the wrong way round, 6.65 ÷ 5.58.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: when is a per-token API cheaper than running the model on your own GPUs, and what else decides it?

keyIdeas.idea: Compare the API's price with your own cost per million at the load you really get (price per GPU hour ÷ millions of tokens an hour), idle and half-full hours included
Count input and output tokens: prompts are billed too
The data leaves under the provider's terms (transfer rules may apply to personal data), and the API's model may differ, so re-test it

recall.model: Compare the API's per-token price with your own cost per million at the load you really get: price per GPU hour ÷ millions of tokens per hour, counting the hours your GPUs sit idle or half full. Count input and output: prompts are billed too. A quiet night on your own GPUs can cost far more per token than the day, and that is where an API often wins. Then add what the sum leaves out: your data leaves under the provider's terms, a transfer rule may apply to personal data, and the API's model may be a different model that must be re-tested on your own cases before you switch.

recall.prompt: Card 2 is switched off at 22:00. The day lines start at 06:00, and a card takes about 3 minutes from switch-on to its first answer. Which switch-on time has it taking answers before 06:00 with the least card time paid?
recall.why: Switched on at 05:50 it takes answers at 05:53, seven minutes early, for 10 minutes of card time. 06:00 gives 06:03 and 05:59 gives 06:02, both late; 05:00 is ready but pays 50 minutes more.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. From Monday 12 October card 2 switched off at 22:00 and on at 05:50 every night, and the report has led with tokens a second per card since: $665 a month saved. Then the winter order came back. At 22:00 on Monday 7 December two night lines reopened, and card 1 took every note and answer alone, as set on the rental company's page: 64 at once. At 23:10 a press lead radioed that the notes were crawling. By hand: 10 ms + 64 × 0.25 ms = 26 ms a step, 38.5 tokens a second for every note, below the day's 55.6. Card 1 wrote 2,462 tokens a second, and the night's cost per million was $0.31, the cheapest we've ever had. The meter said 100%, as always. Tarquin says the night is finally efficient.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the cheapest night per million give the slowest notes, and what should decide how many cards run at night?

keyIdeas.idea: Card 2 was switched by the clock, not by the load, so one card took all 64 answers in 26 ms steps
Fuller steps make each token cheaper but each answer slower; set a limit per card, such as 32 answers at once (18 ms, the day's pace)
Let a load trigger start card 2 when answers at once on card 1 pass the limit, allowing its 3-minute start-up

coldCase.model: The rule switched card 2 off by the clock, not the load. When two night lines came back, card 1 took all 64 answers in 26 ms steps: fuller steps make each token cheap, $0.31 per million, but each answer waits 26 ms for its next token, 38.5 tokens a second, slower than any day. Cost per million is not the only target, so set a limit per card, at most 32 answers at once (18 ms, the day's pace). Then let a load trigger decide: when answers at once on card 1 pass the limit, start card 2, which takes answers about 3 minutes later; keep the clock only for the morning start, with one card as the floor. With both cards on for 64: 18 ms a step, 55.6 tokens a second each, $0.44 per million.
